subtopic: TABLING OF TARIFF BOARD REPORT ON WOVEN FABRICS OF MAN-MADE FIBRES
TABLING OF TARIFF BOARD REPORT ON WOVEN FABRICS OF MAN-MADE FIBRES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have tabled today copies in the two official languages of the report by the Tariff Board on Reference No. 144, together with a transcript of the evidence presented to the board at its public hearings. The report covers woven fabrics of man-made fibres used in the manufacture of garments.
I would like to assure the House that the Tariff Board's recommendations will be carefully considered by the government. Therefore, interested parties who wish to comment on this report should bring their comments to the attention of the Department of Finance as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, if I may I would put the same proposition from an angle, about Which the House may feel differently. Pursuant to Standing Order 43 I ask for the unanimous consent of the House to consider a motion. Under Standing Order 43 I am allowed to make some brief comments and I assure Your Honour they will be extremely brief.
[Mr. Lambert (Edmonton West) .1

The President of the United States, Mr. Nixon, has announced this morning a substantial cutback of Canadian oil exports to the United States east of the Rocky Mountains from the present level of 620,000 barrels a day to 395,000 barrels a day.
Whereas this unilateral action by the United States government in sharply curtailing Canadian oil exports will have a most serious effect on the Canadian economy I move, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles):
That this House discuss today the announcement by the United States government on Canadian oil exports and the response of the Canadian government to this arbitrary and unilateral action taken by the government of the United States.

subsubtopic: ARMING OF U.S. IMMIGRATION AND CUSTOMS OFFICERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Acting Prime Minister. It relates to the fact that for more than a century Canada and the United States have set an example to the rest of the world by maintaining one of the few unarmed frontiers in the world. Does the government intend to protest to the United States government regarding its decision to allow United States immigration and customs officers to carry guns in the exercise of their duty, thus symbolically negating the undefended border concept?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ARMING OF U.S. IMMIGRATION AND CUSTOMS OFFICERS
speechtext: I do not really think that this kind of action would negate the existence of the undefended border between Canada and the United States because I am quite sure that the United States immigration and customs officers will not carry guns in order to prevent an invasion of that country by Canada.

subsubtopic: ARMING OF U.S. IMMIGRATION AND CUSTOMS OFFICERS
speechtext: Would it be to keep out oil?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ARMING OF U.S. IMMIGRATION AND CUSTOMS OFFICERS
speechtext: I regret that there should be weapons in the hands of officers of the government, but this is a decision that the United States must make not only with regard to its relations with Canada but in relation to the security of its own public servants.

subsubtopic: ARMING OF U.S. IMMIGRATION AND CUSTOMS OFFICERS
speechtext: Has the government of the United States given any advance information or explanation to the Canadian government as to why they deem this necessary, and is it the intention of the Canadian government to discuss the matter with the U.S. government in the hope that the former situation may be restored?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: ARMING OF U.S. IMMIGRATION AND CUSTOMS OFFICERS
speechtext: I was not aware until I read the reports or listened to the radio this morning of the action of the U.S. government. The very fact that they did not discuss it with us indicates, I think, that they did not think it related in particular to relations between Canada and the United States.

speechtext: Oh, oh!

He said: Mr. Speaker, the larger portion of the bill before you is required to give effect to the government's decision to introduce legislation to provide for increases in the pensions of retired public servants and their surviving dependants commencing in the month of April, 1970. As the House will recall, that decision was announced by my colleague, the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury), just before the Christmas recess in December, 1969.
As that proposed legislation was to include provision for the escalation of pensions of former Members of Parliament, it was going to be necessary to amend both the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act and the 1965 statute which dealt with retirement from the Senate. The government considered it desirable, therefore, to include in this bill the amendments which it was proposing to Parliament as a result of its review of the report on parliamentary allowances of Emeritus Dean C. A. Curtis of Queen's University. Due to the interrelationship of these two sets of amendments, it had the great advantage of simplifying the drafting of the legislation to combine the two in the same bill.
In dealing with the general escalation question, I do not have too much to add to what the President of the Treasury Board said to the House on the afternoon of December 19. The proposals which are now before you are based on a report by the advisory committee on the Public Service Superannuation Act which examined proposals made to the government for a special contributory plan financed by contributions of the government and employees. That committee concluded that such a plan financed by equal contributions of the government and employees is feasible as a continuing method for updating pensions payable in respect of retired public service employees under the Public Service Superannuation Act.
[DOT] (3:30 p.m.)
Assuming that this bill is approved and receives royal assent before the House rises for Easter, those now receiving government of Canada pensions in respect of employment with the federal government would have their pensions increased as of April 1, 1970. For example, for those who retired in 1969 the increase will be 2 per cent, while those who

Statute Law Amendment Act, 1970 retired earlier will receive larger percentage increases up to a maximum of 42 per cent for those who retired in 1952 and earlier. Again commencing in 1971, pensions may be increased by a maximum of up to 2 per cent in each year, geared to a formula based on the cost of living, if in any year that should be appropriate.
These increases will in turn be financed by additional contributions of one half of one per cent by present employees, contributions that will be matched by the government. Both contributions will go into a special contributory account for funding the additional benefits.
My preceding remarks related primarily to the public service employees in the technical sense, and while representatives of the Canadian Forces and the RCMP attended the meetings of the advisory committee during its study of the subject and the preparation of its report, this committee confined its recommendations to the financing of the escalation of pensions of public service employees.
The decision in respect of the Canadian Forces and of the RCMP Force was taken separately in consultation with those responsible for those forces. The same considerations which led to the acceptance of a joint employer-employee contributory scheme for the benefit both of those already retired and of those retiring in the future in the case of public service employees were recognized as being equally applicable in this case also. The costs involved for present members were partly responsible for the choice of age 60 as the normal commencement age for these increases.
The bill also incorporates an additional change with respect to the Canadian Forces pensions and those of the RCMP. As lion, members may recall, when the Canada Pension Plan came into force those two groups elected to have the superannuation benefits received attributable to military or police service reduced at age 65 by the amount of the Canada Pension Plan payments attributable to that service. Those two groups have now signified that they would like to be treated in the same way as other retired public servants, namely, that their superannuation and Canada Pension Plan benefits be co-ordinated so as to produce somewhat higher benefits. The bill includes an amendment to effect that change.
There are, in addition, a number of special classes of public officials who are also dealt with in the bill. Under the Governor Gener-

The present provision on eligibility for pension after contributing in respect of sessions in three Parliaments has been changed to one of being a member for six complete years. This will undoubtedly mean that some members will qualify after being elected only twice instead of three times as in the past. On the other hand, some members have been able to qualify in as little as 34 years under the present system.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
Dean Curtis also proposed that payment of the full pension be deferred to age 55 with provision of reduced actuarial equivalent benefits payable earlier. The government decided that the principle in the present legislation, which was introduced in 1952, should be retained whereby the pension should be payable immediately a former member qualified. To help fund these payments, the government proposed an increase in the members' contributions to 74 per cent from the 7 per cent recommended by Dean Curtis.
The bill also meets what has been a serious worry to many members in providing annuity benefits for dependent children of deceased members. Under the present legislation, while survivorship benefits are provided for spouses, none are provided for children. This bill provides that an annual allowance of one-tenth of the basic allowance shall be paid to each dependent child up to a maximum, of three, along with the payment to a surviving parent, of three-fifths of the basic allowance. In the case of orphaned dependent children, the bill departs from Dr. Curtis' recommendations which were that the widow's three-fifths should be allocated among the surviving children whatever their number. Instead, the children's allowances are doubled from one-tenth to one-fifth each.
In the case of senators, a parallel change is provided in that those under the Members of Parliament Retiring Allowances Act will contribute on their combined sessional indemnities and expense allowances immediately. Mr. Speaker, the main purpose of part I of this bill is to neutralize to some extent the effects of inflation as applied to certain groups at fixed incomes, namely those on pensions as a result of having served to a pensionable age as civil servants, members of the armed forces, in the RCMP, the Senate, the House of Commons or anyone else covered by schedule A on page 39 of the bill.
We, in the official opposition, are fully in support of the principle of the bill but we have some criticism to offer in that the government delayed so long in introducing it to Parliament. We propose, therefore, that this stage of the bill be as brief as is reasonable so that it will reach the committee in a reasonable time and the committee will have some time to consider it.
Of course in this bill, the government is in the role of an employer and Parliament, therefore, is being asked to make certain amendments and corrections to the conditions of former employees of the government. This bill must receive royal assent by March 25, on our present schedule. Clause 4 of the bill is mandatory and provides that commencing with the month of April 1970, the benefits under the bill shall be paid. Clause 6 provides that these benefits shall be paid at the same time and in the same manner and during or in respect of the same period as the pension payable to the recipient.

My information is that the various pay offices have been and are now engaged in adjusting the April cheques. This government has allowed less than five days since the printing of the bill for an assessment of it. It now allows only 12 days for the rest of the Parliamentary process. Part I is essentially a financial adjustment between the employees of the government, past and present, and the government as an employer. There are benefits to be paid to past and present employees but there are also increased financial burdens to be placed on present and future employees and on the people of Canada who must match the additional contributions of the public service, the RCMP and the armed forces.
To meet the April deadline, this bill must have debate on second reading, be considered in committee, be reported out for consideration on the report stage, get third reading and then go through roughly the same processes in the Senate before it receives royal assent. This timetable can only accommodate government witnesses as to the committee stage. It cannot be expected that organizations representing the public service, ex-members of the RCMP, the armed forces and other organizations will have adequate time to present to the committee whatever their views might be. There is a slight odour of political blackmail rather than participatory democracy in this kind of timetable because it limits debate.
The consideration that Members of Parliament will be able to give the bill in committee will be limited and there will not be as good an opportunity as there should be for those affected by the bill and interested in it to put their views forward to the committee.
Having said that, I say that not only is there not enough time left for its consideration in a reasonable manner but it should have been introduced much sooner because retired civil servants and others have been suffering from the erosion of their pensions for a number of years by inflation. In some cases this has been very unjust.

I want to turn now to Part II of the bill. I note, Mr. Speaker, that it is based in its most important respects on the Curtis report. I commend the government for having appointed Dean Curtis to study this matter of parliamentary pensions because it is a difficult matter. Dean Curtis has had this question under review for about three years now. It is a complicated and difficult task that

is not generally understood by the public. In my humble opinion such a study should be made by an unbiased, objective expert as is Dean Curtis instead of a committee of this House, so that we may have a decision that is fair to the public and to members of the House. In his report Dean Curtis says:
The whole matter of retiring allowances, pension plans, etc., has received a great deal of attention in recent years and has become one of the most important aspects of employment conditions. The great growth in private pension plans, and the social security system in the United States and Canada are all evidence of this. It is therefore appropriate that the position of Members of Parliament under existing plans should be reviewed.
The growth of private pension plans in recent years has been accompanied by the initiation and development of retirement allowances for Members of legislative bodies in the United Kingdom, the United States and Canada. At the present time eight provinces and the federal parliament have established some type of plan.
In earlier times, being a member of a legislative body was regarded as a form of public service which the individual contributed with the obligation to cover the costs involved. Indeed, it was not until 1911 that the British Parliament introduced payment of House of Commons Members. And in Canada the indemnities were always relatively low. The view that such positions were for people of means has given way to the recognition that adequate payment must be made if people of ability are to be attracted to the field-irrespective of their economic circumstances. It is thus necessary to have retirement plans which are comparable with those existing elsewhere.
The situation of members of elected bodies is that their retirement may be involuntary-
That is a polite way of saying members may be kicked out by their constituents. I continue:
-after a relatively short period of service. There is, so to speak, an occupational hazard not common in other occupations. Few people go into public life for the money income involved; indeed the real income of the position comes in the form of prestige, power and the ability to influence decisions.
I sometimes think that backbenchers and members of opposition parties cannot influence the decisions of this government as much as they ought to be able to do. I continue:
In the main, it is non-pecuniary. But this should not obscure the fact that many able and willing people may be disbarred from this occupation because of economic considerations and the risks involved. It is, therefore, the function of the financial returns to people in public life to reduce such economic handicaps to a minimum. It is also true that being a Member of the House of Commons is now a full-time occupation. In earlier days the House sat less frequently and the Members could continue with their usual occupation in some manner. Now, it is nearly impossible for a Member to carry on his usual business or occupation. If he does, something is neglected.
March 10, 1970	COMMONS
I could not agree more with those sentiments. May I point out some of the occupational hazards of being an elected representative? According to statistics available for the last few Parliaments, almost half of Parliaments' membership will fail to qualify for the minimum period of six years for the minimum pension. In other words, almost 50 per cent of hon. members serving will not survive long enough as Members of Parliament to qualify for a minimum pension. The statistics of the last few years also show that not more than 1.5 per cent of the total membership of the House will qualify for the full pension. Only 1.5 per cent of all members here will survive that long as members. Only about 10 per cent of the membership of parliament survives in Parliament as long as 15 years. These statistics, obtained by studying a number of past Parliaments, are quoted by Dean Curtis in the report.
No one should think that when a Member of Parliament finishes his parliamentary career, however brief, he will automatically qualify for the $13,500 pension. The ex-member who qualifies for the full pension will be quite a rare bird. The bill generally follows, in most of the important aspects, the recommendations of the Curtis report, and therefore I agree in principle with it.
As the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) pointed out that the government did not accept the recommendation which states that the qualifying age for a pension should be 55 years. Because that recommendation has not been accepted, half of 1 per cent has been added to the total contribution and members who are under 55 years of age as well as those who are over will now contribute an extra $90 a year. The member may begin to collect his pension immediately on ceasing to be a member, regardless of age. By the nature of things few members will qualify for the pension during their younger years, but there may be some. The additional one half of 1 per cent members will have to contribute, plus the one half of 1 per cent we shall have to contribute to provide for the rising cost of living, will mean that the individual's contribution will be 8 per cent of his income, which is quite a heavy contribution so far as pension plans go. But, as I said, we cannot be judged on the same basis as employees who have security of tenure in their employment and can look forward to a long period in the same employment, probably until their normal retirement age of 60 or 65.

Because Members of Parliament may qualify for a pension when relatively young, some may think that the pension provision is unjustifiably generous. May 1 point out, Mr. Speaker, that individuals are not usually selected by parties or nominated by parties or individuals to represent constituencies in Parliament until they have made some reputation and name for themselves in their own communities. It is usually at the beginning of their most productive years, whatever their profession or business may be, that individuals are drafted by their friends or neighbours to run for Parliament. That being so, hon. members frequently find they have given their best years to Parliament and leave it poorer than when they entered. I am, therefore, delighted to see that the bill will remove the terrible insecurity that has been hanging over the wives and children of Members of Parliament. Too often we have seen cases where serving Members of Parliament have died and left their dependents destitute.

I have spoken about this matter quite a few times in the intervening years, although I have no record of the number of times. It was, therefore, with great appreciation and real delight that I rose that afternoon to respond to the statement of the President of the Treasury Board when he indicated that legislation would be brought in for the escalation of pensions of all federal superannuates, both those who are now retired and those who will retire in the future. I am happy today that the bill before us, in so far as it deals with that aspect of the matter, implements to the full everything that the President of the Treasury Board announced on the afternoon of December 19.

In referring back to what happened on December 19, I say again it was one of the happiest and most exciting moments of my career in this place. I am very happy that we have before us in legislative form what was announced on that occasion. However, Mr. Speaker, I have to admit that the edge of that excitement and happiness has been somewhat reduced by the action of the government in putting another matter into this bill, namely the complete revamping of the Members of Parliament pension provisions. Those who retired that year or earlier will get a 42 per cent increase in their pensions. In January 1971 there will be another increase. If the cost of living continues to rise, there will be increases in these pensions of up to 2 per cent every year from now on. In other words, the formula of the Canada Pension Plan is being applied in this case. That is all good, Mr. Speaker. I welcome it. I have long contended for the principle of universality in pension matters. I am glad to see it is being carried out in this case.

This is a total package. It is one society. We have to stand together on matters of this kind. I expect to be on the committee to which this matter will be referred-I am sure that that will not come as a surprise to hon. members-and I shall certainly go into this matter at the committee hearings. Nevertheless, I think it is a bit raw that a group that was vie-

I must now move on to the other aspect of this bill. Despite the critical comments that I have made, I still welcome the portions of Bill C-194 that deal with the escalation of pensions that have been put in pay as a very desirable piece of legislation. From my standpoint, this aspect is good in itself. It is also good because it sets a pattern. I hope that the Canadian National Railways will be the first to follow this pattern, and that if there are any other emanations of the Crown that need to do so, that they will do likewise. Further, I hope it will not be long before all pensions do the same. Indeed, I want to see it made clear in our pensions standards legislation that a pension is not a pension unless provision is made for escalation. But I say, I welcome this part of the bill.
With respect to that part of the bill that alters and amends-in fact completely recasts-the pension plan for Members of Parliament, I must say this aspect takes the edge off my enthusiasm for this bill. Let me say immediately that I do not think that these wide, sweeping changes should be in this bill at all.
It is perfectly all right to put in this bill, as the President of the Treasury Board said on December 19 he would do, a provision relating to the escalation of pensions of retired M.P.'s, those who are out now. It is also perfectly proper to provide that the pensions of members who are now in the House, once they go out, will also escalate in the same way that all civil service pensions will escalate. But to incorporate in this bill a complete revamping of the M.P.'s pension plan at a time when we are doing only one thing for everybody else does, I suggest, if I may put it mildly, make us look a bit ridiculous.
Although that view may not be shared very widely in this House, I suggest that from the outside the serious question will be asked: How is it that we can do only one thing for all the others, namely escalate the pensions, yet for ourselves we can recast the whole plan, making it much more generous than most other plans that one can find in the pensions field? There are two completely different aspects here. There is what is being done for the civil servants and public employees generally; then there is what is being done for us. Statute Law Amendment Act, 1970 bottom, those on the war veterans allowance and the old age pensioners.
I shall end where I began, by saying that I was delighted on December 19, 1969, with the announcement of the increase in the pensions of retired civil servants. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been a pleasure to listen to the thoughtful exposition of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Macdonald) and the philosophical approach of the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean) that this is a problem of great concern to a large number of Canadians. To a certain degree, it was interesting to hear the views of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) with whom I served on a joint committee of the Senate and House of Commons which dealt with this particular matter a number of years back. It is interesting to note that on Tuesday, January 10, 1967 this House empowered that particular committee to inquire into and report upon the matter of pensions paid to retired civil servants or their dependants under the provisions of the Public Service Superannuation Act. Then, as time went by, our terms of reference were broadened for us by the House so that we could consider the pensions of former members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and former members of the armed forces. That committee, under the chairmanship of the hon. member for Ottawa East (Mr. Richard), held eight meetings, heard 21 witnesses and then with remarkable speed was able to report back to the House and to the other place on May 8, 1967.
The committee unanimously recommended that six things be done. Perhaps it would be worth while to read the portion of the report in which the recommendations were made almost three years ago. The committee recommended:
(a)	it should be capable of quick and early implementation in the form of legislation in the next session of this Parliament;
(b)	any adjustment in pensions should not be limited to a particular date of retirement and should be in addition to any other increase already granted under the Pension Adjustment Act of 1959;
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
I pause there to note that it only took the government of the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) some one
4600	COMMONS
Statute Law Amendment Act, 1970 and a half years to come to grips with the problem. It has taken the government of the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his predecessor almost ten years.
The report continues:
(c)	It should maintain the principle contained in the present legislation that benefits should be related to length of service:
(d)	It should conform to the principle that any adjustment formula should take account also of the time which has elapsed since retirement;
(e)	It should take into account the increase in living costs during that period of time; and
(f)	It should increase the ceilings in the 1959 Pension Adjustment Act.
As I said, with unanimity and after those meetings, on May 8, 1967, the joint committee reported to the respective Houses. Since then, the members of that committee, myself included, have sat in frustration wondering when something was going to be done. On December 19, we heard the announcement from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) that something would be done. Hence, the measure before us now. As I understand from the explanation of the President of the Privy Council, and as I read the special report by Dean Curtis, it is apparent to me that we do not propose to give ourselves or the people of the other place anything. We are going to pay for what we receive under this legislation.
The scheme that is proposed for us is actuarially sound, and I would be very interested to know whether the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has had his enthusiasm dulled or blunted by it. I wonder what other formula he would suggest, instead of throwing to the gallery some sort of general suggestion or hint that all is not well in Parliament and that in some underhanded way we are dealing with benefits for ourselves. I say, sir, that this plan is established on the best of actuarial principles, and when the government rejected the concept of retirement at the age of 55 it was suggested that a pension could be obtained earlier. The very sensible provision was made to tack on another .5 per cent to pay for that benefit to those who did not wish to wait until the age of 55. However, according to the mortality statistics of the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean), some of us have no chance of reaching the age of 55. This may be true, knowing the burden that my colleagues on all sides of the House face with an aggravated situation in the committee system. I, myself, am supposed to be at two committee meetings at this time, and would be at one of them if I 
DEBATES	March 10, 1970
did not have to be here. I do not think that one could apply to us, in view of the very special hours that we work and the very special responsibilities that we have, the concepts that one would apply to people in grey flannel suits in the suburbs of Canada who live nine to five lives. So I feel no twinges of conscience about the formula that has been devised for members of this and the other House. It is actuarially sound and I think also just.
I do have some question in my mind about the formula by which civil servants now working help, in effect, to underwrite the increases for those who are retired. Let me not be misunderstood on that point. I do not quarrel with the increases rising up to 42 per cent for those who are retired. I think that is justice. I am only sorry that it did not happen at least three years ago when the committee to which I referred made its report. But the fact is that it should be a matter of principle for Parliament and the government that nobody now working should be asked to assume a part of the load for those who are retired. I agree that civil servants, the RCMP and members of the armed forces should pay for their own increases at two percent per year. They should pay into that fund because, on an actuarial basis, they will be receiving the benefit from it. But there is a portion of the increased levy that will be used to pay those who are retired, and I suggest that that sum should be paid out of the whole treasury of Canada.
I further make the argument-and I did raise it once in the House-that to proceed as the government has proceeded with the retired civil servants by putting part of that burden on present civil servants in effect makes the present employees of the government subject to a special tax. I say, sir, that all of us should be paying that tax. Why do I make that argument? Am I just in making it at all? The statment is that some of the money being raised by the special levy will go to help those who have already retired.
When the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) made his announcement to the House on December 19 of last year he listed a good number of points, but that particular piece of information was not given by him. However, in January of 1970 the personnel policy branch of the Treasury Board secretariat made to the bargaining agents in the public service proposals regarding public service pensions. I obtained in Halifax the copy of them that I am now holding from one of the bargaining groups. I also believed that
March 10, 1970

other Members of Parliament should enjoy this special information, and notice of motion for the production of papers No. 361 on our Order Paper dated February 3, 1970 requests:
That an Order of the House do issue for documents sent by the Personnel Policy Branch, Treasury Board Secretariat, to those groups which are the bargaining agents for employees in the Public Service (including Armed Forces and RCMP), relating to the statement of the President of the Treasury Board on December 19,	1969, in the
House of Commons concerning extra benefits for superannuates.
Neither the minister nor anyone has as yet tabled that particular document. I cannot understand why, and I regard that as a discourtesy. I asked for a document to be tabled well in advance of this debate, so it could be made available to all Members of Parliament who have not had the advantage of reading the document that I happen to have in my possession. I am surprised that the government did not accede to my request.
What does the paper say with regard to this point? I am saying again that it indicates the government is putting a special tax-which may be minute-on those still working to cover those who are retired. At page 3 of the document I referred to it, it is stated:
The entire amount at the credit of the Superannuation Account is required to meet the liabilities undertaken with regard to the purchase of the basic pensions payable under the Public Service Superannuation Act. There is no surplus in the account which could be used to pay for the increases to present pensioners. Consequently, the escalation funds have to come from the plan's contributors-the federal government and its employees.
Farther on, the following statement is made:
Initially, the additional contributions will be seen as offsetting increases in pensions already in pay. But the plan looks both forward and back.
There are only a very few civil servants in Canada, apart from those who do the active bargaining with the government to obtain these collective agreements, who are aware that they are in fact being asked to pay what I call a special tax. This aspect was never put up to them, in any way, shape or form. When I raised the matter in the House of Commons initially there were some members of the press who saw me about it afterwards. Apparently, they did not think the point was of sufficient importance to bring to the attention of the people, for example of the Ottawa area, where there are a great number of public servants. Yet to me, it is an important matter of principle.
Statute Law Amendment Act, 1970 [DOT] (4:50 p.m.)
I state again that I don't object to the increases, but I think the increases for those who have retired from public life and are entitled to the benefits under this bill should be a matter to which all taxpayers of Canada should contribute. This special increase properly looks after those who will retire later on but, in my opinion, improperly helps bear the cost for those who have retired already.
There are several other points I think will bear examination in the committee. I note that there is provision in the bill for military and civil servant retirements that are enforced by the mental or physical condition of those being retired. However, as I read the bill there is no provision for those who may be compulsorily retired, that is those people in the public service and in the Armed Forces who are being pushed out before their normal terms of service elapse when they would expect to draw whatever pensions were available to them. And I think that this is a point, particularly with the government having a retirement policy that is somewhat aggravated in these days, that we will have to follow up.
I regret, too, that the government could not have persuaded the Canadian National Railways or its predecessors, the Intercolonial Railways-I think there is a Prince Edward Island Railway in there as well-to give some increased benefits to their retired employees. But perhaps by setting the example in this bill, the railways can be persuaded to take steps that a normal, good intentioned employer would take.
Sir, I can say that I welcome the bill with the exception that I still think it is not a dangerous but a wrongful principle to impose a special tax, as I have argued is being imposed in this case and as I am sure I will be able to prove in the committee when we study the bill, or have somebody prove it for me. But I welcome it. I think it is long overdue. These steps should have been taken at least three years ago, and should have been taken as a matter of principle by the government and by Parliament to keep faith with their retired employees in these inflation infested times.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ELIMINATE TRAINING FLIGHTS AT INTERNATIONAL AIRPORTS
speechtext:
that Bill C-33, respecting Pilot Training Flights by International and Regional Air Carriers at International Airports in Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
[DOT] (5:00 p.m.)
He said: Mr. Speaker, the under lying purpose of this bill is to restrict pilot training flights by international and regional air carriers at international airports in Canada. It provides that, subject to the provisions of section 17 of the National Transportation Act, the Air Transport Committee of the Canadian Transport Commission may order the cessation of all such training flights.
March 10, 1970
I am sure many hon. members will realize the pressing need for legislation such as this to provide a measure of relief, small though it may be, for those living in communities surrounding international airports all across the country. However, during this debate today I will deal mainly with the problem as it affects persons living near the Vancouver airport in my constituency of Burnaby-Rich-mond, although similar situations have existed, or do now exist, at the other international airports in Canada.
Broadly put, the problem would be said to be one of pollution-noise pollution. Now, since the first airports came into existence, aircraft noise has been a source of irritation to persons living nearby. When bigger, more powerful aircraft, especially jet airplanes, began to fill Canadian skies the problem became more and more acute. Nowhere has this been more true than at the Vancouver airport. It is now almost 39 years since greater Vancouver's first airport was opened on almost the same location that the present $32 million terminal complex now stands on Sea Island in the municipality of Richmond. In the intervening years, the original airport which boasted a single 2,400 foot long runway and a total land area of 475 acres has grown to a base which includes more than 3,000 acres and has a main east-west runway 11,000 feet long. This growth was made necessary by the very great increase in the use of the Vancouver facility. Vancouver international airport is one of Canada's busiest centres of aviation activity. In 1967 it recorded 112,826 aircraft movements. Included in this total were 86,000 scheduled flights carrying 1.8 million passengers.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, it is not difficult to appreciate that with such a great deal of air traffic the seemingly inevitable noise problem has increased accordingly. This fact has caused very real hardship to those persons living in relative proximity to the airport. It is, to say the least, very difficult to live anything like a normal life when jet aircraft are constantly in flight just overhead. But these people of whom I speak are reasonable people. They fully understand and appreciate the vital role which air transport plays in our society. They do not wish to stand in the way of the advances our technology has produced. They merely ask that we begin to turn this technology to the task of solving some of the problems that earlier advances have produced.
Undoubtedly one such problem is the question of noise caused by aircraft during land-
Pilot Training Flights Cessation Act ing and takeoff. I remain unconvinced that this government is moving quickly enough to force commercial carriers to adopt vitally needed noise abatement measures for jet aircraft engines. Nor is it advancing rapidly enough the required research program in the whole field of noise pollution. Nevertheless, some progressive steps have been taken. For example, I give credit to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) for instituting new aircraft noise abatement measures at Montreal international airport. These measures involve the curtailment to an absolute minimum of aircraft movement to and from Car-tierville airport which, I might add, was for five consecutive years Canada's busiest airport in terms of total traffic.
This curtailment permits increased use of the runway on the northwest side of the Montreal airport which means that many flights which had been using the southeast runway and passing over a dense residential area, are now making their approaches and departures over the Cartierville airport and the less built up area adjacent to it. As a result, there is a substantial reduction in noise in Ville St. Laurent, a highly concentrated residential area. I have asked the minister, and do so again, to implement similar action on Sea Island at the Vancouver airport. There are presently plans to construct a second major runway at the airport. If these plans are brought to completion, many flights which at present land and take off over the residential areas of Richmond could be diverted to the new runway with the result that approaches and departures would take the aircraft over the Fraser River and adjacent industrial area rather than nearby homes. The present delay in constructing this new runway can not be tolerated any longer. The target date of 1975 is completely unacceptable to this member.
As I have said, Mr. Speaker, the persons living near the Vancouver international airport are reasonable people with a reasonable request. They want the government to see that the same advanced technology that can produce such flying wonders as the 365-ton Boeing 747 is now turned to ensuring that the noise factor from these jetliners is kept to the absolute minimum. They recognize that increased air service is both necessary and desirable. With this necessary service there is, unfortunately, bound to be for some years to come a certain degree of discomfort from aircraft noise. This fact is accepted. But note here that I have said "necessary service".

March 10, 1970

Pilot Training Flights Cessation Act There is one practice, one further addition to the general level of hardship, which neither they nor I think should have to be endured. This practice is the use of Vancouver international for pilot training by commercial carriers. My bill seeks to eliminate this additional burden.
CPA is presently the worst offender with regard to pilot training flights at the Vancouver airport. This company conducts 34 per cent of its training flights there with only the most rudimentary restrictions on flight activity. At this time their training flights are subject only to a voluntary effort to avoid noise sensitive areas. How effective have these voluntary efforts been? Allow me to quote, Mr. Speaker, from a letter I received concerning an incident which occurred one evening late last year. My constituent wrote:
I would ... like an answer why CPA when it was training this night at precisely 8:06 p.m. dove at my house with a four-motor jet, cut the engine power hack, let the jet sink then gave full power to the engine and flew off into the dark.
Another letter which came to my office in January read in part:
Take note that CPA jet No. CF-CPS drove us nuts on Saturday, January 10, 1970, from approximately 9:00 a.m. until noon, and on January 11, CPA jet No. CF-CPI from approximately 7:00 p.m. until 10:00 p.m. Also on the latter date the jet made two extremely low passes over our houses, cut engine power and then gave it full power. These passes were at 7:40 a.m. and 8:40 a.m. Sunday morning.
It seems clear enough, Mr. Speaker, that these so-called "voluntary efforts" CPA is supposed to be undertaking are not enough.
Now I recognize that the company has need to conduct a pilot training program. The argument of myself and my people is not against training flights per se, we just cannot understand why Vancouver international must be used for such flights when there are facilities which are, or soon can be made, adequate at airports near less highly populated centres. One such facility I should mention is Abbotsford airport which is already used as an alternate air field when Vancouver international is fogged in.
Even if CPA would agree to eliminate weekend flights as a gesture of concern, and a show of good faith to the community, feelings might not run so high on this issue. My opinion and that of the residents of the area is that weekends are an especially undesirable time for these training flights, especially on Sundays. For some families Sunday is the only day they have to rest and relax. To be awakened at 7 a.m. on a Sunday morning by

aircraft noise is not only an unpleasant experience; it is an abrogation of the individual's right to peace and quiet in his own home. One lady wrote to me as follows:
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
On Sunday we rarely ask people to visit, because in the last year the weekend air traffic has made normal conversation impossible. The same situation applies to phone conversation, you don't chose to do the phoning at your own convenience, but rather when the fewest jets will be passing over.
However, CPA has rejected any plan to do away with week end flights. I have put this proposal to CPA on a number of occasions, but as the replies have not been positive we have no choice but to seek approval for legislation which will make it possible for an agency of the government to force commercial carriers such as CPA to do what they should already be doing as good corporate citizens. This is the aim of the bill before this House.
As I said earlier, Mr. Speaker, my remarks have concentrated on the conditions at the Vancouver International Airport but the basic issue under discussion, that of noise pollution, is not just regional in nature. Its scope is nation-wide. Therefore, I hope that this bill, as one measure that should become part of a total program to combat this form of pollution which threatens not only our physical health but our mental health as well, will receive wide support from all sides of this House of Commons.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO ELIMINATE TRAINING FLIGHTS AT INTERNATIONAL AIRPORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset may I congratulate the sponsor of this bill for his concern on behalf of his constituents. Indeed, noise is a form of pollution around airports. In Canada and throughout the world, this form of pollution is becoming very serious and methods must be found to control it.
The sponsor of the bill has not introduced a measure dealing with noise, or with noise as a form of pollution. The bill suggests indirectly that noise is a form of pollution. The purpose of the bill as set out in the explanatory note is:
-to restrict pilot training flights by international and regional air carriers at international airports in Canada.
I said the other night that a bill introduced by a colleague of the hon. member from British Columbia was good in intent but wishy-washy, and neither clear nor definitive. The same might be said here. Considerable attention has been given to pollution from noise,
March 10. 1970

and much information is available to those who are interested in finding it. Airlines are constantly striving to reduce the noise of their aircraft's engines, particularly around major airports, but stopping flying training at international airports and moving it to regional airports such as Abbotsford is certainly not the answer to the problem. May I say that if the people in Vancouver, Toronto, Montreal, Calgary or Edmonton object to flying training in their areas, we shall be very happy to accommodate training pilots at Halifax International Airport, because every time an aircraft lands or takes off it means that money is left in our economy; and we welcome that. Perhaps that remark may sound facetious; at any rate, we would welcome flying training activities in the Halifax area.
Although I congratulate the hon. member for his concern about the people living off the end of one of the busy Vancouver runways, I suggest that what he is advocating or suggesting is not really possible. It may be very desirable; by the same token we may all like to drive Cadillacs, but we do not all have Cadillac incomes. Flying training is a very necessary part of transport and communication in Canada today. With the ever-increasing jet traffic at our airports has come the vital need of making absolutely certain the pilots of these aircrafts are competent and completely familiar with changing techniques that may involve new methods of blind approach as well as operations in the air traffic control tower.
Briefly, Mr. Speaker, the basis of my concern is the tragic mid-air collision a short time ago at the airport the hon. member referred to and the reaction of the people who viewed it. There is no indication of what caused the accident and we must be careful not to assess responsibility and blame. The best way to avoid accidents like this is by constantly upgrading the capability of local traffic controllers and the pilots who fly not only private aircraft but the regional, national and international air carriers as well. Air traffic control towers at our international airports report to Ottawa an ever-increasing load factor. Perhaps I might put on record one or two statistics that will support in a general way what the hon. member is attempting to do. I have in my hand a service bulletin of the Aviation Statistics Centre, put out by the Dominion Bureau of Statistics. The document is dated October, 1969 and bears the number 8705-501. It reads in part:
In 1967, 7,304 civil aircraft registered in Canada with a valid certificate of airworthiness, flew 2,136,614 hours.
Pilot Training Flights Cessation Act
That is an awful lot of flying in anybody's language. I continue quoting:
Of this total 2,098 commercially operated aircraft flew 1,400,625 hours or 65.6% and 4,722 privately owned aircraft amassed 643,118 hours or 30.1% of total hours flown.
These figures have increased by substantially more than 14 per cent since October, 1969. I, therefore, suggest that the increased air traffic at airports has increased and not diminished the necessity for our constantly upgrading the skills of pilots. Most experienced pilots need to take what are known as check rides every so often. As airports become more congested, senior and advanced pilots must be able to upgrade constantly their flying skills and techniques, and to practise simulated approaches at our airports. Department of Transport statistics indicate that in September, 1969, there were 8,603 simulated approaches in this country, whereas in the previous year there were only 7,170. In other words, simulated approaches are increasing at the rate of 1,500 per year. Many of these approaches were undertaken to upgrade the skills of commercial pilots; some were check rides, and others were undertaken to break in, so to speak, new pilots.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
It is impossible to overstate the necessity to maintain the high level of safety that both Canadian Pacific Air Lines and Air Canada have achieved. These pilots must train in airports where there is total control in terms of the ever-increasing amount of traffic at the airports involved. This can only be done at fully equipped airports. In addition to a tower, it is necessary to have precision approach radar as well as fire and crash crews standing by. These men train in highly sophisticated equipment. Although it is dangerous, it is a procedure that must be followed if the pilots of our national carriers are to maintain the very high standard that the Canadian air traveller enjoys today.
Another point I wish to make is that training in flying aircraft must be done in the safest possible manner. While it may be a bloody nuisance to the people living at the end of a runway to have planes flying overhead at eight-thirty or nine o'clock at night, the fact is that this is probably the safest time of the day to do this training. This training should not be carried out during the peak hours. I refer to early morning, mid-morning, mid-day peaks as well as the rush hour between four o'clock and six o'clock p.m.
4606	COMMONS
Pilot Training Flights Cessation Act These are the times when the airports are congested and when there is a maximum amount of operational activity.
Perhaps the member feels the situation has become a serious problem. Possibly an airport should be established somewhere in Canada, maybe in the Prairies, where this type of training could be carried out with the conditions at our international airports being simulated. All material necessary in the event of an accident or emergency could be available at such an airport. However, such a plan would be very costly. This may be the reason the hon. member did not suggest it in his bill.
The bill has merit, although I frankly do not know where our national or regional air carriers could carry out their flight training if this were not done at our international airports. I do not know what other airports in Canada would have the necessary facilities. For these reasons, I feel I must oppose the bill. We recognize the traffic loads at international airports are ever-increasing. The question of safety is much more important than the question of noise, although noise has a prominent place in connection with airports.
I wish to make a further observation about airports and training activity as it applies to the private sector. The Canadian Owners and Pilots Association, which represent virtually all private fliers in Canada, contends that the public image of private flying and the suggestions of near mid-air collisions, etc., is not very good. Indeed, it has been harmful to what is a very healthy and stable Canadian industry. Official government accident investigation reports originating in the United States on collisions between airliners and private aircraft have shown that, in some cases, the airliner overtook or was on a collision course with the private aircraft. Therefore, we must be careful what we do. We must not do anything that will downgrade or cut back the amount of time available to train pilots of our national air carriers. They must be constantly prepared to cope with private aircraft.
Because of the highly sophisticated manner in which our national air carriers operate, and the very lagging ground support facilities, we must be very careful not to move too quickly on bills that would in any way restrict the amount of supervised and controlled time that even some of our most senior and experienced national and international pilots require. They require this training as much as anyone else.
No matter how serious the hon. member might be about the problem of noise, I sug-

gest it would not be in the interest of the Canadian travelling public if this House were to prohibit in this type of flight training at the only airports where it can be carried out.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not often a member introducing a private bill indicates so clearly his reasons for presenting the bill. If this bill is passed, I am sure it will eliminate the problem with which he is faced. However, it will accomplish little other than to meet the objections of the residents who live at the end of runways.
The problem is the lack of urban control around airports. I remember when Malton Airport was considered to be a long way out in the country, yet people have been allowed to build around that airport. It is now like a downtown airport. These people have a legitimate cause for complaining about the noise, but I feel the noise is only beginning. When the new supersonic jumbo jets come into operation later this year, those people living within eight or ten miles of the airport will find the noise totally intolerable. Instead of just finding the noise objectionable, they will be blown right out of their beds at eight o'clock on a Sunday morning.
I agree with the previous speaker that pilots must be trained in the type of aircraft they will be flying. There are only a limited number of airports in Canada which have the sophisticated equipment necessary for training. We have not restricted training flights on this type of aircraft, nor have we restricted training flights on much larger aircraft. I am referring to the initial pilot training that is undertaken.
Hon. members will recall reading a week or so ago about a very unfortunate accident which occurred in British Columbia where a small plane apparently collided with a commercial aircraft. Happily-if I can use that term in connection with a disaster-it did not have a more detrimental effect on commercial aircraft, otherwise the toll might have been considerably higher.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I commenced my remarks on Bill C-194 by saying that I would make a few general observations and not a lengthy speech. I pointed out, with regard to the first part of the bill
Statute Law Amendment Act, 1970 which deals with the 2 per cent escalation in the pensions of retired civil servants, RCMP officers, judges and other persons, that there appears to be very little objection to it even though under this bill people who retired in 1952 would receive a 42 per cent increase in their pensions. I think most people realize that over the years these people have suffered as a result of the increase in the cost of living.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) stated that December 19, when the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Drury) made the announcement, was a happy day. The hon. member had a right to be happy because over the years he has persistently set forth the legitimate claims of pensioners across the country, and more particularly those of civil servants.
The hon. member's persistence has paid off: he had the right to be happy on December 19. He pointed out that some retired civil servants may have suffered if their pensions were so low that they had to avail themselves of the war veterans allowance. If this increase will result in a reduction in the war veterans allowance, I think the government should take steps to take care of the situation.
With regard to the second part of the bill, which is the recasting of the pensions of the Members of Parliament, if I understood the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre correctly his main objection to it was that the benefits which would be conferred upon retired Members of Parliament would be too generous. I could point out to the hon. member that a similar plan exists in the Ontario legislature, the members of which receive roughly the same benefits as those proposed for the Members of Parliament on their retirement.
It may be said, however, that two wrongs do not make a right. I follow this up by saying that the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean) made a very salient argument this afternoon when he pointed out that surveys have indicated that only 1.5 per cent of the members of the House will have had 25 years of service which would entitle them to a pension of 75 per cent of their salary, and that only 10 per cent will have attained 15 years of seniority. That is quite indicative. I am sure the hon. member for Malpeque knows it is not only political attrition that takes place with regard to Members of Parliament and is a hazard of being a Member of Parliament. Physical attribution also takes place, because Members of Parliament today

Statute Law Amendment Act, 1970 are not to be compared with those of 25 years ago. Some 25 years ago the members of this House sat for three, four or five months of the year. We now find ourselves sitting for eight, nine and ten months of the year and facing a very heavy burden of work.

It may be the hon. member got his spiritual figures mixed up. As a young socialist, Mr. Speaker, feeling the difference between the old socialists and the generation gap, I thought he could have used a more appropriate scripture and said, as the Galilean carpenter said, "I come that you may have life and have it more abundantly." Today we young socialists have to think in terms of surpluses, and the distribution of the surpluses is so important in society today.
When you think of what we as Canadians are doing with regard to the surplus of wheat, I think we stand condemned for not distributing the surplus to underdeveloped and under-


privileged countries. One thing about the old socialists is that they came up in times when there were shortages. We are now in times of surpluses and technological change, and it is up to us to distribute these surpluses to the advantage of all people within the community.

It is not enough to have the spirit: you must have the talent. Many people who are talented are making far higher incomes and receiving far greater pensions in the other fields they are pursuing. subtopic: STATUTE LAW (SUPPLEMENTARY RETIREMENT BENEFITS) AMENDMENT ACT. 1970 MEASURE TO SUPPLEMENT PENSIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the reason that we are considering this bill this evening results from one fundamental difficulty. It is a matter to which I have referred on previous occasions, and that is that the programs of the pensions for the public service, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, the armed services, the Members of Parliament and others subject to this bill have never been funded. In other words, while there is such a thing as a public service superannuation account and an armed services superannuation account as book entries, the payments therefrom are a charge against the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
There is no segregation of actual moneys, no fund invested in the hands of trustees, and there is no growth in the fund due to investment. All that there is is the provision of the contributions from members to each of these pension funds, and the contributions of the appropriations by the government. Then in view of the progressive increase in the cost of living over the years and the very natural demand, and the right thereto, by the participants in any of these pension funds to increase their return so as to meet the exigencies of the day and maintain the standard which had been promised them, there is an undertaking that when you give a man a pension scheme, you will give him a standard of living. There is that implication, and it has been denied.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
I recall-I believe it was about 1958-that this House gave an increase in pensions to retired public servants and, I believe, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police for those who retired prior to 1953 and whose pensions were below a certain level, which I think was $3,000. This was a sort of bandaid operation and I think it was wrong not to tackle the problem properly. Mind you, there were other problems in 1958 which I think would have caused a terrific change. It seems to me that the more we delay, the more difficult will be the change-over.
Doing it this way, with a provision for an automatic cost of living escalator which is fixed, if we continue with the present scale of inflation-and there is no guarantee that we will not-there will be a mounting deficiency each year of something in the nature of 3 per
Statute Law Amendment Act, 1970 cent or almost 4 per cent. This means we will get the same pressures in a matter of a few years. However, if there had been a funded program for these pensions, there could then have been determined actuarially the increase in the amount of the pensions based upon the increase of the funds through earnings, and therefore through capital appreciation. The funds should not only be in government bonds because they have gone down tremendously, particularly in the past two or three years.
In any event, we would not have this fundamental difficulty of having to come along at this time in order to relieve the very real distress of those thousands and thousands of members of the public service and the armed forces, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police and also, unfortunately, many of our colleagues who have departed from this place, or their widows, who are living in relative penury today. All sorts of ad hoc arrangements have been made to take care of some of the cases to the point that what we had up to a few years ago was scandalous, and it is just short of that now.
We are now asking the public service-ourselves in a different way, but let us say the public service-and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to pay an additional premium into a separate account which I suppose one could call an inflation account. It will put into a separate account an amount which will be then paid to those persons who are the most deserving under the scale proposed in the legislation, where the cases are the hardest. It will also provide that the present members of the public service and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who will retire in the years to come will have this automatic 2 per cent escalator, all because of the additional premium that they pay.

Mr. Speaker, it takes courage to introduce a bill of this kind in the House of Commons, especially at a time when one branch of government is begging for restraint while another is saying we should try to do something where there is need. The devil can quote scripture to his purpose and hon. members may decide, if they like, whether I am devil or saint because I intend to refer to a little scripture myself by saying that the workman is worthy of his hire, and thou shalt not muzzle the ox that treadeth out the corn. I hope my friends to the left are listening; They know about the corn. Then I say: Lo unto you scribes and pharisees, hypocrites. You speak one thing and do another. You are willing to take the money but not the political risk of demanding that which you know is just and fair.
When we consider the spending of $15 billion of the Canadian people's money, it represents a tremendous responsibility on the part of those who sit in this chamber. They form the board of directors of a tremendous corporation, the all-powerful state. I am surprised that the criticism comes from that corner of the chamber where they bow down in their hypocrisy and believe that the people of Canada will support it. What utter nonsense! In some countries of the world I suppose we would be called commissars. Do they live at the bottom of the heap, do they have the private yachts on the Sea of Aza and the private villas on the Baltic or do they eat the caviar and drink the vodka while the poor peasants sweep the streets of Moscow. What hypocrisy, indeed! I will give you a little more scripture: I would that ye were either cold or hot.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has stood up once a week for the last ten years begging for a square deal for civil servants. In one form or another I have been a civil servant for many years. This is a time not to be a civil servant. I think perhaps we should have placed the question of our salaries before a private corporation of some kind. A corporation might not have been afraid to take the responsibility of seeing that members get a square deal from the Canadian people.

You might say, "You were only a policeman once and you walked the beat for 50 cents a day". Yes, I did. You might then ask, "But were you proud of that?" I fought overseas, and it is strange to be told by people who did not fight overseas about my duty to

It is only we who are so mean as to say that those who serve the country well should take the bottom of the heap. When you say that, it is from the depths of hypocrisy because if you are worthy of your salary in the House of Commons, I do not know what your salary should be. It is a poor trick to divide our salaries into parts and say that one part is for expenses, another part is salary and the third part is indemnity. If we are unable to come to a decision on what is a reasonable amount, let us hand over the responsibility of making that decision to a group of university professors, or let it be done by computer.
There are inequities right now in the House of which we are all aware and which members to my left could well point out. Does anybody within sound of my voice think that everybody should get the same expense account as a member who covers 2| million square miles in an area where there are no roads and no transportation facilities except for the airplane and the kayak? Should he be expected to cover the frozen Arctic on $6,000 a year when it is impossible to hire an aeroplane with a pilot for less than $200 a day, as anyone who has been there would know?
I had the great honour of being the member for Athabasca when I had only 100,000 square miles to cover. I was expected to do it on $6,000 a year. I could not do it then, and I could not do it today. This is very different from having an Ottawa riding and getting the

same $6,000. One can say there is an obvious inequity there. However, I would not agree that the man who represents an Ottawa riding is getting too much, because if you got out the score sheet you would probably find that he has expenses about which my friends in the press never talk. How would anyone like three or four school buses full of people driving up to one's door? One is expected to pay for their lunches three or four times a month. This costs money.
My friends to my left talk about the just society just as much as government members. What would they do about this situation? Would it be possible for a poor labouring man to pay for the lunches of 200 school children out of his own pocket? This is the best pay I have ever had in my life. But if I am doing my work here in the House as I should, I would not hesitate to say that the people of Canada might well take a good look at what I do and decide whether or not I am overpaid. How much does it cost to be a good Member of Parliament without living in the fleshpots, doing one's work, answering one's mail and fighting an election without taking mean or crooked money? It is not one election; we have had six elections in ten years.
Are you supposed to go begging when you write a letter? Are you supposed to thumb your way through the Arctic and pick on the poor natives in the kayaks to get you around this great, dynamic, young country of ours; or should we sit in committee of the House and thrash out this thing like gentlemen? We have computers today. How much does it cost to travel through the Arctic? Let us find out, and stop this business of saying that some of us make a little more and some of us make a little less.

We are not paid on commission. If we were on commission we would have a great deal more money. We are spending $15 billion a

What is a member's take-home pay? For 10 years I have listened to references about money that I am getting for noth-21774-151

People who write these stories do not know how much I am taking home as a public servant, which I consider to be the highest honour one can receive in the country. As Members of Parliament we get a very small percentage of the salary received by some civil servants who are contributing little or nothing to the welfare of this country.
While I was sitting here making notes I made a list of some of the things we should be doing. We are responsible for the defence of Canada. Have we any defence in Canada? If we were being paid for the defence of Canada, perhaps we should take a 30 per cent cut in our pay and go home. We are here for the formation and improvement of our laws. I am not too sure that some of the laws we pass are any great improvement, despite the hard work we may have done in committee.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
We are supposed to be ombudsmen for an average of 75,000 people apiece, yet the government thinks it necessary to have regional desks. If members of the cabinet need regional desks, it is because they are not working us properly, we are not working properly ourselves or we have not sold the idea of why we are here and that we are doing our job. I do not think we need regional desks. I happen to think I am ombudsman for the 77,000 people who sent me here. Maybe that is why they sent me back here five times. I say to hon. members, if you want to qualify for your full pension, be an ombudsman for your 75,000 people and they may send you back here more often than you want to come.
Then there is the question of having two homes to maintain. I have two homes to keep up. We want family men in this chamber. We don't want just bachelors; we don't want just spinsters. We want family men, who represent the greatest cross-section of the people of Canada. If you are a family man and a Member of Parliament, you have two duties to fulfil. You have to think of your family at home, the children going to school, training to be nurses or going to university. In fact your wife has to think of these things a great deal more than you do while you devote your time to the service of the nation. In return she bathes in only a little reflected glory. That little reflected glory gets less and less every time someone gets up in this House and says we are not worth the money, as more than one hon. member has done already. I would like to hear much more from men who are going into debt in the service of our country

March 10, 1970

Statute Law Amendment Act, 1970 than from men who do not have to rely on inadequate pensions because they have private fortunes, such as most of us do not enjoy.
Then, too, we have a certain amount of entertaining to do, whether we like it or not. Some of us are a long way from our constituencies and we are only too pleased, when people from home come to see Parliament Hill, to take them around. But some hon. members have busloads of people arriving, and this can become a considerable financial burden unless one happens to have a private fortune.
If you do your work as a Member of Parliament, you are responsible for the political education of the public. Any time you are asked-and it is often at your own expense-you have to go and talk to farmers, tradesmen, fishermen or any other group of people who want to hear you, who want to know how you do your work and the difficulties you encounter in doing it. One of your jobs is to keep people abreast of democratic progress in Canada. All this costs money. You cannot travel from here to northern Alberta, a distance of 2,500 miles, and back without a considerable outlay from your private resources.
The Member of Parliament is not expected to be on a salary. Nobody has ever called our pay a salary, yet that is what it is. The Member of Parliament has to put up with a broken business or professional life. But we won't be hypocritical about that. Of course I knew that was going to happen when I came down here. But putting the shoe on the other foot, do the people of Canada want me to suffer unduly, financially, if I do the job? I do not think so. I think this is one area where if you take the public into your confidence, tell them the whole story, tell them how much it *costs you to live, how much it costs you to support two homes, how much it costs you personally to fight elections on their behalf- if you are not fighting elections on their behalf, why are you here?-they will see the merit in the case. After all, this is a democracy.
How many men have become rich by coming here? I know of none, and I think that is a credit to this House and to the people of Canada. Only cynical people think that being a Member of Parliament is a short cut to a fortune. I will tell you how innocent I am in this regard. I do not know any of my friends who have made money by being Members of


Parliament. Such a case has not come to my attention. I am naive enough to believe that this is representative of almost all, if not all members of the House of Commons. So, Mr. Speaker, what are we being so shy about? Unless you are a supporter of the successful government of the day when you retire, you can expect no after-reward. As a matter of fact, by being a Member of Parliament you disqualify yourself from many lucrative jobs, and in fact without loss of pension rights you cannot take a job in the direct pay of the government of Canada once you have been a Member of Parliament. This is not even logical.
I believe that Parliament is a good school for the training of public servants. If a man spends two sessions here, works on the committees, takes part in all the discussions, has the experience of meeting men from all over the country, he would have to be a dull fellow not to have learned to be a better civil servant. Yet from the very terms of our work and the terms of our pension scheme we disqualify ourselves from further service to the country.
I am not whining or complaining. I am just trotting out into the open some of the things that have been behind closed doors for too long. It should be placed on the record that we get $12,000 a year subject to income tax, which in a great many cases means approximately one-third off, resulting in $8,000 take-home pay. I have just outlined some of the expenses which no Member of Parliament can escape. Further, the Member of Parliament is donating his time. I think the people of Canada want to know about these things. Of course, I have received letters saying, "Don't you dare raise your pay. Sell the wheat first, Look after our affairs first." That is a very normal, natural, human reaction. But I do not honestly think the people mean that, particularly if they know how conscientious most of us are, the long hours we work, how hard we work and what our financial condition is.
I consider it a brave move, an unpopular move on the part of the government, to bring this thing out in the open at a time like this. The need is great to update our pay and allowances. I hope that when the measure reaches committee we will have no double talk. If the members there cannot come to a consensus to put this scheme into statutory form, I hope we will hand it over to an independent commission as soon as possible and make an attempt once more to take the whole matter out of the realm of seamy politics where I think it has been for far too long.
