I had been going in the hole for $1,000 a year for five years, so I thought $10,000 a year was a lot of money. But I was surprised how much I could spend and how many calls there were on it. I was continually going to the bank to sign another note. I think this is relevant to the extent of what one is doing and what your expenses are.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want to talk about wages but I can assure you we are going to be very important people in this country-right now we are not-if we decide our salaries should be $100,000 a year. Then we will be the most important people in this country. We may not be the most popular, but we will be the most important.
Over the years we have seen members come and go. This is an odd job; it is the kind of job where a member has to divorce himself from everything. A member who is really serving in this House-some do and some do not-has to be here before nine o'clock in the morning. I do not usually fit into that category because it is very difficult. But he should be here before nine o'clock or the staff will not be doing anything; and he should be here until the late show at 10.30 p.m. This means that he is limited to meeting the general public on the weekend if he can get to his riding for that purpose. It is not a normal job and the fact that there are only 264 members and not too many people trying for positions is an indication that it has some hazards.
Since I came here I have heard many people say that this or that cannot be done, or that the Canada Pension Plan was an impossibility. Everybody laughed at me when I raised it, but only two years later when the government said they were going to implement it, nobody voted against it. I have seen this sort of thing on many occasions. My interest, Mr. Speaker, is to win for everybody the maximum possible pension. There are many unknown quantities in any pension plan. If somebody says, "Pension plans have always gone broke and the Canadian people have to pay more money all the time," there is something wrong with the plan. We have had two calamities to our pension plans: we had the calamity of 1958 when we lost 50 per cent or more of the members, and the calamity of 1962-63 when we again lost 50 per cent or more of our members. But these are not normal circumstances. The hon. member who spoke previously said that we had six elections in ten years and the turnover was con-
siderable in that length of time. I do not think we anticipate that situation in the foreseeable future, so our pension plan has not been a difficulty to the Canadian public, and we are making our contributions.
Some time ago, Mr. Speaker, I was offered the opportunity of participating in the pension plan of the union where I had previously been employed. That plan was five and five-5 per cent paid by the employer and 5 per cent paid by the employee. Being employed outside that plant I would have had to pay 10 per cent of my present salary of $12,000 plus $6,000. When I looked at $1,800 a year, I decided I could not afford it. It seems to me a pension plan hinges on what a person can afford to pay. No matter whether the employer is paying a share or not, it has to be paid from wages. The plan has to be self-supporting. It is not like the unemployment insurance plan where occasionally we get into a situation where we have to add money to it.
Someone asks, and rightly so, whether we should not do something about the actuarial study that regulates the establishment of that kind of fund. So long as the fund is solvent and no one can point to any error in the calculations connected with the plan, I think we ought to be able to contribute to as large a pension as we can afford.
[DOT] (9:50 p.m.)
Several factors connected with the pension plan for a Member of Parliament ought to be considered. One of them is, as Dean Curtis pointed out in his report, the difficulties members may face on being re-elected. Some members who served here for relatively short terms have been unable to find suitable employment, the difficulty being psychological more than anything else. It is hard to be at the top, then be thrown out and start at the bottom. It is much easier to work when you are at the top than when you are at the bottom. Some members who have been in this position have had difficulty. Dean Curtis suggests that perhaps we ought to give these people a generous grant for the first year after their defeat. I think the best way of doing this is by providing ourselves with an adequate pension scheme that will not cost the taxpayers additional money.
The qualifying time for a minimum pension has been reduced to six years. I think that is unduly generous because I saw nothing wrong with the three-term provision. I am amused to see people who during five years here have served three terms. When the hon. member

for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) first came here, he fought three elections in one year. Immediately after his first election he was forced to fight a by-election, and within eight or nine months he again fought a general election. He really has been elected to Parliament three times.

speechtext:
If Members of Parliament are willing to make larger contributions, and if the plan can be introduced in such a way that it does not impose an additional financial drain on the treasury, I see nothing wrong with it. I believe every man should be entitled to a retirement pension which will give him a reasonable standard of living. Every man on retirement should be entitled to live in the manner to which he is accustomed. Some people ask: Why should a man making $50,000 a year be paid $25,000 a year on retirement? I don't know why he made $50,000 in the first place; it is none of my business and I do not give a damn. I do not expect ever to be in that category, but the more power to that man. I do not say he is worth it, but that is his income. He must justify it to some people. His wife will be used to maintaining a certain standard of living. When he retires she will want to continue at that standard and ought to be entitled to do so.
I should like to see in this country an adequate retirement plan for every Canadian. I should like to see insurance companies and the annuities branch eliminated from the retirement field, and the Canada Pension Plan extended to the point where every Canadian can pay into it enough money to assure for himself a decent standard of living in keeping with his best income during his life. maintopic: INDIAN AFFAIRS-NORTHERN QUEBEC- TRANSFER OF JURISDICTION OVER ESKIMOS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposition I wish to raise this evening arises from a question asked of the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) a few days ago which related to the matter of consultation with the Eskimo people, particularly in Quebec, and what the minister meant exactly by "consultation". At no time has the government or the minister attempted to define what is meant by "consultation". The word has been much misused, abused and distorted by the government. I think it probably originated in the mind of the former minister, the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Laing), who developed the idea of the initial round of consultation conferences with the native people coincidentally with the 1968 election campaign. I realize that is an argument.
Anyone examining even cursorily the so-called white paper on Indian Affairs which
March 10, 1970
4628	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion supposedly resulted from this consultative conference would agree that the word "consultation" is meaningless. In many respects the ideas presented in the paper that evolved as the result of the June 25 meeting last year bear no resemblance to the ideas expressed by the native peoples at the so-called consultative conference. In the minds of Indian and Eskimo peoples of this nation, "consultation" is a word mouthed by government members and is meaningless. They see consultation merely as a process of one-sided conversation, where they listen to people whose minds about the course to be taken are already made up.
We attempted to obtain information from the minister the other day, particularly with respect to the Eskimo people in Quebec who have unequivocally told the government that they do not want jurisdiction over their affairs to be transferred to the province of Quebec. They want to decide for themselves what jurisdiction they will come under. The minister was asked if he would accede to that request of the people. He was asked to listen to grass roots conversation and to pay attention to the needs of the people who would be affected by any such change. The minister refused to budge from his declaration that he would consult with the people. At no time did he indicate he would pay attention or give heed to the intentions and desires of the people.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
This matter was put in perspective today by an answer the Parliamentary Secretary gave to the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Brown) in reply to a question regarding the closing of a Mohawk centre at Brantford. The Parliamentary Secretary made his reply with some emphasis and flair. He said, "The closing of the Mohawk institute"-to which the hon. member for Brant had referred-"was after detailed consultations". He made a previous reference to the consultations and used the phrase, "with the consent of the Indians concerned". The phrase "with the consent of the Indians concerned" was said with such elaboration and emphasis it almost appeared as though the unusual had happened. That consultation did not take into account the views of the people concerned.
If the Parliamentary Secretary was at liberty to say that the views of the Indian people with respect to the Mohawk institute had been listened to and acceded to, by the same token the minister, who has far more power
[Mr. Howard (Skeena).l

and authority, should also take advantage of his privilege and right to say in this House unequivocally and clearly to the Eskimo people in Quebec that the government does not want to impose upon them the jurisdiction of the province of Quebec and objects to it strenuously.
The government should say to those Eskimo people that it is their fundamental right to make that determination. They should be told they are under the jurisdiction of the federal government, will stay there and attention will be paid to their request. The government should say it respects and honours the decision of the Eskimo people and that it will sever any further negotiations and discussions with the province of Quebec in that regard.
Instead of that, the minister talked about the matter of consultation without defining what he meant. He refused to budge from his previous position and tell the Eskimo people who are directly concerned that he would accede to their request, listen to their views and honour their position. In the absence of any such declaration, we can only conclude that these discussions and negotiations with the province of Quebec will continue. The discussions have been carried on for some years; they commenced before this government took office. The purpose of the negotiations is to work out a solution which is contrary to the views of the Eskimo people.
If the Parliamentary Secretary will say, as he said with respect to the Indian people at Brantford and the Mohawk institute, that the views of the people will be listened to and a decision made based upon the request of those people, they will understand clearly where they stand and will respect the government. In the absence of a declaration of that sort, I am afraid the views of the people are going to be overridden.

Mr. Speaker, that is what we are doing at the present time, and when we have received a report from the officials now engaged in such consultations, we shall be in a position to inform the House on the situation.
I do not have time to refer to the question asked by the hon. member for Skeena on February 25, but it appears at page 4081 of Hansard and my minister gave exactly the same answer. In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, all I can say is that the federal-provincial team is presently still in the area, as my hon. friend knows, consulting with the native peoples. I am informed that it will be a matter of two or three weeks before the consultations are concluded. They will then, of course, report to the respective governments.
I would emphasize that this is a federal-provincial team which is consulting with the Eskimo people. When a report is received, it will then be the responsibility of the respective governments to consider the recommendations of the report, and if further action or consultation is necessary it will be taken. But at some point a decision will have to be made by those in authority.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly glad 21774-16

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion that the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Sharp) is here this evening because I am quite sure he appreciates the urgency of the question of Canada's role in helping, through the United Nations, to get birth control information and family planning to those countries of the world that need it badly.
I was quite shocked when I read in the paper the other day that the program of the United Nations Fund for Population Activities this year has been jeopardized, so the story goes, by differences within the Canadian cabinet over whether or not we should participate in a program that we had agreed to help. Under this program, the United States, Britain, Sweden, Japan and the Federal Republic of Germany, together with Canada, were expected to contribute a total of $15 million for the budget of the United Nations Fund for Population Activities.
Evidently there is a hold-up, and according to the press this hold-up is in the Canadian cabinet. According to this story, the cabinet has not made up its mind about the program although birth control in this country is legal and although we would not be forcing it on any country that did not want it. The Canadian cabinet at that time had plainly made up its mind that Canada should carry out its agreed part of the program.
[DOT] (10:10 p.m.)
As I say, I know the minister appreciates the desperate urgency of this situation in the kind of world we have where it took several million years to reach the 2 billion mark in population, which we had in the mid-1980s. They tell us that by 1975 the figure will be doubled to 4 billion people, and that if we go on without any other thing intervening there will be 14 billion people in the year 2035. The likelihood is that there will not be all those people because of a number of very tragic things that will happen. For one thing, poverty breeds poverty and we know how it does. The capital growth of the underdeveloped countries will be brought to a standstill long before that time, because poverty will feed on the few resources they have and there be no chance for them to get ahead. Then there will be continued exacerbations in gross inequalities, and the fear that world income will be going to the developed nations, with all the potentialities for racial hatred and war that that situation will bring.
Also, famine will break out and the people will be dwarfed by the prolonged and dread-
4630	COMMONS
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion ful famines of the future. In the next place, the low income and prevalence of hunger in the poorer countries can only mean a continuation of political instability. It is the underdeveloped nations that are most often racked with military coups, civil wars and violent revolutions; and if uncontrolled violence occurs, it can only increase instability. Then there will be diseases. Of course, we now know above everything else the dangers that exist in pollution. They are on a terrible scale, and in all forms imaginable.
It is for this reason I ask the minister-as I asked him earlier today, not knowing that I would be having the opportunity this evening-if he can make some statement as to whether or not this conflict is now resolved within the cabinet and when we can expect it will be resolved. I ask the question because I believe that the matter of world population and family planning can no longer be left to the old-fashioned cliches and shibboleths of yesterday. This is too important a matter to be left to old doctrines any longer: it is a matter of world survival.

Mr. Speaker, I regret very much I was not here when the hon. lady put forward her question the other day, but I read Hansard with considerable amusement. I recognize, of course, that the hon. lady, in spite of the mirth that was generated, was very serious in what she had to say. She has today had the opportunity of elaborating her views at greater length and in greater quiet than existed at that time.
The government is actively engaged in elaborating policy in respect of family planning both domestically and internationally. Perhaps I might point out to her as evidence of our great interest that CIDA, the Canadian International Development Agency, has obtained the services of Dr. George F. Brown as special adviser in public health and population. Dr. Brown is well known as a specialist in international family planning programs.
I think this indicates that we are not lacking interest in the matter.
I think she will also agree that our international policy must be related to our domestic policies. It would be quite improper for Canada to apply different standards domestically and internationally. We would quite rightly be the point of criticism, that somehow we felt that Canadians were to be treated differently from other people in respect of this kind of activity and policy. I am sure

DEBATES	March 10, 1970
that my friends in the NDP would be the first to condemn such hyprocrisy.
The first step in elaborating a domestic policy in respect of family planning has already been made, as the hon. lady has said, by an amendment to the Criminal Code regarding the dissemination of information on contraceptives, and the government is presently considering what else it should be doing in this field. When we have reached a conclusion in this matter we will be in a position to elaborate our international policy.
In order to indicate that we are not the only important country that is having difficulty making up our minds in this field, I would point out that the United Nations Fund for Population Activity to which the hon. member has referred has only very recently been re-organized. It is only now in a position to accept expanded contributions. Few countries have made contributions. Some countries including Britain, Japan and the Scandinavian countries have the matter under consideration. In this connection I simply want to repeat that the government recognizes the importance of family planning programs and is actively considering what its policy should be both domestically and internationally.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 6 I posed a question to the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing. I asked him whether or not the federal government intends to make direct loans to municipalities and regional governments to assist them in assembling and servicing land for urban growth in line with the proposal of the Hellyer task force. Mr. Speaker did not allow the question at that time, and therefore I pose it again tonight. The report of the task force on housing and urban development points out the following:
On the basis of all the evidence and impressions before it, the task force believes that municipal assembly and servicing of land would produce major reductions in land costs in both the short and long-term while encouraging and assisting effective urban planning. Therefore, in summary, the task force recommends that:
Municipalities or regional governments, as a matter of continuing policy, should acquire, service and sell all or a substantial portion of the land required for urban growth within their boundaries.
The federal government should make direct loans to municipalities or regional governments to assist them in assembling and servicing land for urban growth.
March 10. 1970

It was in line with that recommendation that I asked the question the other day. I am sure the government realizes it is not good enough to go about the country with a task force. Grand words concerning what the government may be doing or thinking are not enough. Philosophy is not good enough. Tours of any description across the country are not good enough unless there is active participation by the government in this field. Possibly the government is considering putting this type of money into land assembly projects, but to date the municipalities have been unable to meet the rising costs with which they are faced and therefore cannot be expected to come up with any project in respect of land assembly for urban growth.
At the same time, I am sure everyone here realizes that municipal taxation cannot rise any more: it is at the highest level it has ever been. It would be impossible for the municipalities to attempt to tax the people in order to pay for the type of land assembly that is necessary. With this view in mind, I pose the question and would appreciate an answer this evening.
